conditions.name: Weakened immune system
conditions.intakeQuestion: Is your immune system weakened by a condition or medicine, for example an organ transplant, chemotherapy, HIV, or strong steroid or immune-suppressing medicines?

flags.label: St John's wort
flags.why: It can weaken ciclosporin, a transplant medicine, and some HIV and cancer medicines.

flags.label: probiotics
flags.why: Probiotic microbes can cause serious blood infections when the immune system is weak. Only use one if your doctor advises it.
alsoWhy: Probiotics have been linked to serious blood infections, mainly in people who are very ill or have weak immune systems.

flags.label: berberine
flags.why: In kidney transplant patients it raised blood levels of ciclosporin.

flags.label: turmeric
flags.why: Tell your doctor before taking turmeric if you take tacrolimus, a transplant medicine.

flags.label: ashwagandha
flags.why: It might interact with medicines that suppress the immune system.
alsoWhy: It might interact with medicines that dampen the immune system.

flags.label: herbal supplements
flags.why: After a kidney transplant, some herb interactions can make anti-rejection medicines work less well.

flags.label: omega_3
flags.why: Very high doses (about 1.5 g or more of EPA plus DHA for several weeks) might dampen immune responses.

flags.label: vitamin_b1
flags.why: People with HIV have a higher risk of low B1.

habits.title: Bring your supplement bottles, or a photo of the labels, to appointments
habits.why: Your care team can look up each ingredient for safety.

doctorQuestions: Which supplements are safe with my medicines?
Are probiotics safe for me?
Do I need any vitamin levels checked?

conditions.name: Epilepsy
conditions.intakeQuestion: Do you have epilepsy or take medicine to prevent seizures?

flags.label: St John's wort
flags.why: It can weaken seizure medicines such as phenytoin and carbamazepine.

flags.label: vitamin_b9
flags.why: Some seizure medicines lower folate, and folate supplements might lower the medicine level. Check with your doctor before taking it.
alsoWhy: Folate and some seizure medicines affect each other's levels.

flags.label: ashwagandha
flags.why: It might interact with seizure medicines.

flags.label: cannabidiol (CBD)
flags.why: CBD is listed as possibly interacting with valproate.

flags.label: vitamin_d
flags.why: Vitamin D is listed as possibly interacting with phenytoin. Ask your doctor about the right amount.
alsoWhy: Some seizure medicines can weaken vitamin D's effect. Ask your doctor about a blood test.

flags.label: vitamin_b6
flags.why: B6 can lower some seizure medicine levels, and some seizure medicines lower B6.
alsoWhy: High doses (200 mg a day) may lower blood levels of phenytoin and phenobarbital.

flags.label: antacids with calcium, magnesium or aluminium
flags.why: These are listed as possibly interacting with phenytoin.

flags.label: vitamin_b7
flags.why: Taking seizure medicine for at least a year is linked to lower biotin levels.
alsoWhy: Some seizure medicines lower biotin levels.

flags.label: vitamin_b9
flags.why: If you are planning a pregnancy or in early pregnancy, UK guidelines advise a higher prescribed dose (5 mg a day) for people taking anti-epileptic medicines.

habits.title: Take your seizure medicine every day and do not change it without advice
habits.why: Missing doses or changing treatment can lead to seizures.

habits.title: Do not drink too much alcohol
habits.why: Too much alcohol can increase the risk of seizures.

conditions.name: Migraine
conditions.intakeQuestion: Do you get migraines?

flags.label: magnesium
flags.why: Magnesium is probably effective for preventing migraines, with modest benefit in trials. Trial doses (up to 600 mg) are above the 250 mg safe maximum for supplements, so ask your doctor first.
alsoWhy: Migraine trials used up to 600 mg a day, which is above the supplement limit.

flags.label: vitamin_b2
flags.why: Riboflavin is probably effective for preventing migraines. 400 mg a day cut attacks by about two a month in one trial.
alsoWhy: 400 mg a day has been studied to help prevent migraine. That is far above daily needs, so agree it with your doctor first.

flags.label: caffeine (including energy drinks and pre-workout products)
flags.why: Too much caffeine can trigger migraine attacks.

habits.title: Keep a migraine diary
habits.why: It can help you find your triggers.

habits.title: Eat at regular times, sleep well and stay hydrated
habits.why: Skipping meals, tiredness and stress are common triggers.

habits.title: Exercise regularly and limit alcohol and caffeine
habits.why: These are advised to help manage migraine.

conditions.name: Menopause or perimenopause
conditions.intakeQuestion: Are you going through the menopause or perimenopause, or have you been through it?

flags.label: St John's wort
flags.why: If you have had breast cancer, it may interact with tamoxifen, blood thinners and seizure medicines.

flags.label: black cohosh
flags.why: There is some evidence it may ease hot flushes, but products vary, safety is uncertain and interactions have been reported. Rare cases of liver damage have been reported. See a doctor if you get dark urine or tiredness.

flags.label: isoflavones
flags.why: There is some evidence they may ease hot flushes, but products vary and safety is uncertain.

flags.label: vitamin_a
flags.why: Over many years, more than 1,500 µg a day may weaken bones. Keep preformed vitamin A below this.

flags.label: iron
flags.why: After menopause needs drop to 8 mg; take iron only if a blood test shows you need it.

flags.label: boron
flags.why: One small study found boron raised estrogen after menopause; another found no change. The effect on health is unclear.

flags.label: calcium
flags.why: Eat calcium-rich foods such as milk, yoghurt and kale to protect your bones.
alsoWhy: Needs rise to 1,200 mg a day after age 50; food first.

flags.label: vitamin_d
flags.why: Vitamin D helps keep bones healthy. Taking a supplement is advised.

habits.title: Do weight-bearing and resistance exercise
habits.why: Helps keep bones healthy after the menopause.

habits.title: Cut down on hot flush triggers like spicy food, caffeine, smoking and alcohol
habits.why: These can trigger hot flushes.

doctorQuestions: Is HRT an option for me?
Are herbal remedies safe with my medicines?
Should my bone health be checked?

conditions.name: Heavy periods
conditions.intakeQuestion: Do you have heavy periods, for example needing to change pads or tampons very often, or bleeding through to clothes?

flags.label: iron
flags.why: Heavy periods may cause about a third of iron-deficiency anaemia in women.
alsoWhy: Heavy periods are a common cause of low iron. Guidelines advise a full blood count for everyone with heavy periods.
Heavy periods are a common cause of low iron; ask for a blood test before taking iron.

habits.title: See a GP if heavy periods stop you doing daily activities, or you often feel tired or short of breath
habits.why: These can be signs of low iron or another cause that needs checking.

conditions.name: Regular or heavy drinking
conditions.intakeQuestion: How many alcoholic drinks do you usually have in a week, and do you sometimes drink a lot in one go?

flags.label: kava
flags.why: Do not combine kava with alcohol. Kava has been linked to rare, serious liver injury.

flags.label: valerian
flags.why: Valerian should not be taken with alcohol or sedatives.

flags.label: vitamin_b1
flags.why: Up to 80% of people with long-term heavy drinking develop low thiamin, which can damage the brain. Ask your doctor about thiamin.
alsoWhy: Alcohol lowers how much B1 you absorb and store. Heavy drinkers should ask a doctor about B1.

flags.label: vitamin_b9
flags.why: Alcohol reduces how well the body absorbs and uses folate.
alsoWhy: Alcohol lowers folate absorption and speeds its loss.

flags.label: magnesium
flags.why: Alcohol dependence can lower magnesium.
alsoWhy: Low magnesium is common in people who drink heavily.

flags.label: zinc
flags.why: 30 to 50% of people with alcohol use disorder have low zinc.

flags.label: vitamin_b6
flags.why: B6 levels tend to be very low in people who depend on alcohol.
alsoWhy: Alcohol lowers B6 levels.

flags.label: vitamin_b3
flags.why: Heavy drinking can lead to low niacin.

flags.label: vitamin_b7
flags.why: Long-term drinking lowers biotin absorption.

habits.title: Keep to no more than 14 units a week, spread over 3 or more days
habits.why: This is the UK low-risk drinking advice for adults.

habits.title: Have several drink-free days each week
habits.why: This helps if you want to cut down.

doctorQuestions: Would thiamin or other vitamins help me?

Are my medicines safe with alcohol?

conditions.name: Training hard or competing in sport
conditions.intakeQuestion: Do you train hard or compete in sport most weeks?

flags.label: protein
flags.why: Protein supplements and high muscle mass can make a common kidney blood test less reliable. Tell your doctor if you take them.
alsoWhy: Athletes may need 1.2 to 2.0 g of protein per kg of body weight a day; up to about 2.0 g/kg is considered safe.
Regular strength training works best with about 1.2–1.6 g per kg a day.

flags.label: creatine
flags.why: May help strength and power in short, hard efforts, but often causes water weight gain. Few safety concerns at usual doses.

flags.label: caffeine (including pre-workout products)
flags.why: Up to 400 mg a day is not usually dangerous for healthy adults. Too much can cause a fast or irregular heartbeat and poor sleep.

flags.label: multi-ingredient sports supplements
flags.why: Ingredient amounts vary widely between products, and makers rarely fund good research on them.

flags.label: potassium
flags.why: Heavy sweating and dehydration make potassium pills riskier; get potassium from food and drinks instead.

flags.label: chromium
flags.why: High-dose chromium in workout products has been linked to rare muscle and kidney damage.

flags.label: iron
flags.why: Athletes can lose extra iron through sweat and foot impact. Correcting iron-deficiency anaemia improves work capacity.

flags.label: vitamin_b2
flags.why: Vegetarian athletes are at higher risk of low riboflavin.
alsoWhy: Hard training puts extra demand on B2. Athletes who avoid dairy and eggs are most at risk.

flags.label: vitamin_c
flags.why: Under heavy training, 250 to 1,000 mg a day halved colds in trials. Men should stay under 1,000 mg.

flags.label: carbohydrates
flags.why: Endurance athletes need enough carbohydrate to perform well.

habits.title: Aim for 1.2 to 2.0 g protein per kg of body weight a day
habits.why: This range is suggested for athletes and is considered safe for healthy people.

doctorQuestions: Do I need my iron checked?
Is creatine or caffeine safe for me?

medicines.name: Metformin

interactions.label: vitamin_b12
interactions.effect: Long-term use can lower B12, more so at higher doses and over longer time. This can cause tiredness, a sore red tongue, pins and needles or anaemia.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor about a B12 blood test now and then, and straight away if these symptoms appear. Do not stop metformin on your own.

interactions.label: goldenseal
interactions.effect: In a study it lowered metformin levels by about a quarter, which could weaken blood sugar control.
interactions.action: Avoid unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: berberine
interactions.effect: May add to the sugar-lowering effect, and it can change how the body handles some medicines.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor before using it with metformin.

interactions.label: chromium
interactions.effect: May add to the sugar-lowering effect.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor first; check your sugar more often.

interactions.label: alcohol
interactions.effect: Drinking alcohol raises the risk of a serious side effect called lactic acidosis and may lower blood sugar.
interactions.action: Limit alcohol and ask your doctor how much is safe.

medicines.name: Insulin and sulfonylureas (for example insulin, gliclazide, glimepiride, glipizide)

interactions.label: chromium
interactions.effect: May increase insulin sensitivity and raise the risk of low blood sugar.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor first and check your sugar more often.

interactions.label: berberine
interactions.effect: May add to the sugar-lowering effect of these medicines, so blood sugar could drop too low.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor before using it.

interactions.label: fenugreek
interactions.effect: Large doses may cause a harmful drop in blood sugar.
interactions.action: Avoid supplement doses unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: vitamin_b3
interactions.effect: Large doses of niacin can raise blood sugar.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor before high-dose niacin; your sugar may need closer checks.

interactions.label: coq10
interactions.effect: CoQ10 may interact with insulin.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor first.

interactions.label: alcohol
interactions.effect: Alcohol can cause low blood sugar, sometimes hours later.
interactions.action: Check your sugar after drinking and ask your doctor what is safe.

medicines.name: Warfarin

interactions.label: vitamin_k
interactions.effect: Changes in vitamin K intake can make warfarin work more or less.
interactions.action: Do not take vitamin K supplements. Keep vitamin K foods steady week to week.

interactions.label: St John's wort
interactions.effect: It can weaken warfarin, so clots are more likely.
interactions.action: Do not take it with warfarin.

interactions.label: vitamin_e
interactions.effect: Can increase bleeding risk with warfarin, especially at high doses.
interactions.action: Avoid high-dose vitamin E unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: ginkgo
interactions.effect: May increase bleeding risk.
interactions.action: Avoid unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: garlic
interactions.effect: Garlic supplements may increase bleeding.
interactions.action: Avoid supplement doses; food amounts are fine.

interactions.label: coq10
interactions.effect: Listed as interacting with warfarin.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor first.

interactions.label: ginseng
interactions.effect: Listed as interacting with warfarin and may affect clotting.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor first.

interactions.label: omega_3
interactions.effect: Fish oil at 3 to 6 g a day usually does not change warfarin much, but your INR (blood clotting test) should be checked from time to time.
interactions.action: Tell your anticoagulation clinic before starting.

interactions.label: turmeric
interactions.effect: May increase bleeding risk with warfarin and other blood thinners.
interactions.action: Avoid supplement doses unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: echinacea and goldenseal
interactions.effect: Listed as possibly interacting with warfarin.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor first.

interactions.label: echinacea and goldenseal
interactions.effect: Listed as possibly interacting with warfarin.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor first.

interactions.label: cranberry juice and products
interactions.effect: UK advice is to avoid them while taking warfarin.
interactions.action: Do not have cranberry juice or cranberry products.

medicines.name: DOACs, blood thinners (for example apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban)

interactions.label: St John's wort
interactions.effect: Listed as not mixing well with apixaban and rivaroxaban. With dabigatran it is expected to lower drug levels, and taking them together should be avoided.
interactions.action: Do not take St John's wort without asking your doctor. Do not take it with dabigatran.

interactions.label: ginkgo
interactions.effect: May increase bleeding risk with blood thinners.
interactions.action: Avoid unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: garlic
interactions.effect: Garlic supplements may increase bleeding.
interactions.action: Avoid supplement doses.

interactions.label: turmeric
interactions.effect: May increase bleeding risk with blood thinners.
interactions.action: Avoid supplement doses unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: vitamin_e
interactions.effect: Can reduce platelet clumping and may raise bleeding risk with blood thinners.
interactions.action: Avoid high doses unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: all vitamins, supplements and herbal products
interactions.effect: Your doctor may need to change doses or watch you closely for side effects.
interactions.action: Tell your doctor or pharmacist about every supplement.

medicines.name: Antiplatelet medicines (for example aspirin, clopidogrel)

interactions.label: St John's wort
interactions.effect: With clopidogrel it can raise drug levels and bleeding risk.
interactions.action: Do not take it with clopidogrel unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: ginkgo
interactions.effect: Herbs that affect the blood, such as ginkgo, may cause problems with clopidogrel.
interactions.action: Avoid unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: garlic
interactions.effect: Garlic supplements may increase bleeding, especially with aspirin.
interactions.action: Avoid supplement doses.

interactions.label: vitamin_e
interactions.effect: Can reduce platelet clumping and may add to bleeding risk.
interactions.action: Avoid high doses unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: omega_3
interactions.effect: High-dose fish oil can have a mild antiplatelet effect, less strong than aspirin.
interactions.action: Tell your doctor if you take high doses.

interactions.label: horse chestnut seed extract
interactions.effect: Products containing aesculin may add to bleeding risk with aspirin or other blood thinners.
interactions.action: Avoid unless your doctor agrees.

medicines.name: Levothyroxine (thyroid hormone)

interactions.label: calcium
interactions.effect: Calcium carbonate can stop levothyroxine being absorbed.
interactions.action: Take them at least 4 hours apart.

interactions.label: iron
interactions.effect: Taking iron at the same time can clearly reduce how well levothyroxine works.
interactions.action: Take them at least 4 hours apart.

interactions.label: vitamin_b7
interactions.effect: Biotin can affect thyroid blood test results.
interactions.action: Tell your doctor before blood tests.

interactions.label: St John's wort
interactions.effect: Listed as not mixing well with levothyroxine.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor first.

interactions.label: chromium
interactions.effect: A small study found chromium reduced levothyroxine absorption.
interactions.action: Ask your pharmacist how to space them.

interactions.label: antacids
interactions.effect: Antacids and other indigestion treatments are listed as not mixing well with levothyroxine.
interactions.action: Take at a different time; ask your pharmacist.

interactions.label: fiber
interactions.effect: Foods with soy, walnuts and dietary fibre may affect how levothyroxine works.
interactions.action: Keep your routine the same each day.

interactions.label: ashwagandha
interactions.effect: May raise thyroid hormone levels and might interact with thyroid medicines.
interactions.action: Avoid unless your doctor agrees.

medicines.name: Statins (for example atorvastatin, simvastatin, rosuvastatin)

interactions.label: red yeast rice
interactions.effect: Some products contain a statin-like drug, with the same possible side effects (muscle, kidney and liver damage) and interactions.
interactions.action: Do not take it with a statin unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: St John's wort
interactions.effect: Can weaken some statins, such as simvastatin.
interactions.action: Avoid unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: vitamin_b3
interactions.effect: Added to a statin in large trials, high-dose niacin did not lower heart events and caused more side effects.
interactions.action: Do not add high-dose niacin unless a specialist advises it.

interactions.label: vitamin_d
interactions.effect: Statins might not work as well with high-dose vitamin D.
interactions.action: Keep vitamin D within usual amounts unless your doctor advises more.

interactions.label: green tea extract
interactions.effect: Can lower blood levels of atorvastatin.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor before using it.

interactions.label: grapefruit juice
interactions.effect: Too much grapefruit juice can raise the chance of side effects with atorvastatin.
interactions.action: Have no more than 1 or 2 small glasses a day, and check your own statin leaflet.

interactions.label: coq10
interactions.effect: Research does not show that CoQ10 reduces muscle pain caused by statins.
interactions.action: Talk to your doctor about muscle pain.

medicines.name: Stomach acid reducers: PPIs and H2 blockers (for example omeprazole, lansoprazole, famotidine)

interactions.label: vitamin_b12
interactions.effect: These medicines can reduce B12 absorption from food.
interactions.action: Ask about a B12 test if you take them long term.

interactions.label: magnesium
interactions.effect: Long-term PPI use (usually over a year) can cause low magnesium.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor about a magnesium blood test.

interactions.label: iron
interactions.effect: These medicines reduce iron absorption; iron tablets may work less well.
interactions.action: Tell your doctor if you are being treated for low iron.

interactions.label: calcium
interactions.effect: Calcium carbonate is absorbed less well with low stomach acid unless taken with a meal.
interactions.action: Take calcium carbonate with food, or ask about calcium citrate.

interactions.label: St John's wort
interactions.effect: May stop lansoprazole working as well as it should, and is listed as not mixing well with omeprazole.
interactions.action: Do not take it with these medicines.

medicines.name: Antacids (for example calcium carbonate, magnesium or aluminium indigestion remedies)

interactions.label: iron
interactions.effect: Calcium-based antacids may get in the way of iron absorption.
interactions.action: Take iron and calcium products at different times.

interactions.label: all medicines and supplements
interactions.effect: Calcium carbonate can affect other medicines taken at the same time.
interactions.action: Do not take calcium carbonate within 1 to 2 hours of other medicines.

interactions.label: calcium
interactions.effect: Calcium-based antacids add to your daily calcium. The upper limit is 2,500 mg a day up to age 50 and 2,000 mg a day after that.
interactions.action: Count antacids in your daily calcium total.

interactions.label: magnesium
interactions.effect: Magnesium in antacids counts toward the 250 mg a day safe maximum from supplements and medicines. Too much is more likely if kidneys are weak.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor if you have kidney disease.

interactions.label: chromium
interactions.effect: Antacids reduce chromium absorption.
interactions.action: Take them at different times.

medicines.name: Tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics (for example doxycycline, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin)

interactions.label: calcium
interactions.effect: Calcium binds these antibiotics so less is absorbed.
interactions.action: Take calcium products at least 6 hours before or 2 hours after ciprofloxacin. Timings differ by antibiotic, so check with your pharmacist.

interactions.label: iron
interactions.effect: Iron binds these antibiotics so less is absorbed.
interactions.action: Take iron 3 hours before or 2 hours after doxycycline. Check timing for other antibiotics with your pharmacist.

interactions.label: zinc
interactions.effect: Zinc binds these antibiotics.
interactions.action: Take the antibiotic at least 2 hours before or 4 to 6 hours after zinc.

interactions.label: magnesium
interactions.effect: Magnesium binds these antibiotics.
interactions.action: Take the antibiotic at least 2 hours before or 4 to 6 hours after magnesium.

interactions.label: multivitamins with minerals
interactions.effect: Minerals in multivitamins can reduce antibiotic absorption.
interactions.action: Space them as for the single minerals; ask your pharmacist.

medicines.name: ACE inhibitors and ARBs (for example ramipril, lisinopril, losartan, candesartan)

interactions.label: potassium
interactions.effect: These medicines reduce potassium loss in urine and can cause high potassium.
interactions.action: Do not take potassium supplements unless your doctor prescribes them.

interactions.label: potassium salt substitutes
interactions.effect: Salt substitutes that contain potassium can raise potassium.
interactions.action: Do not use them without talking to your doctor.

interactions.label: iodine
interactions.effect: Potassium iodide with ACE inhibitors can raise the risk of high potassium.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor before taking potassium iodide.

interactions.label: licorice root
interactions.effect: Even small amounts of licorice root products have been linked to severe side effects in people with high blood pressure.
interactions.action: Avoid licorice supplements.

interactions.label: ashwagandha
interactions.effect: Might interact with blood pressure medicines.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor first.

medicines.name: Potassium-sparing water tablets (for example spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride)

interactions.label: potassium
interactions.effect: These medicines can raise potassium, and potassium supplements may not mix well with them.
interactions.action: Do not take potassium supplements unless your doctor prescribes them.

interactions.label: potassium salt substitutes
interactions.effect: Potassium salt substitutes can raise potassium levels further.
interactions.action: Avoid them; ask a doctor or dietitian.

interactions.label: magnesium
interactions.effect: These medicines reduce magnesium loss in urine.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor before magnesium supplements.

interactions.label: iodine
interactions.effect: Potassium iodide can raise potassium with these medicines.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor first.

medicines.name: Thiazide water tablets (for example bendroflumethiazide, indapamide, hydrochlorothiazide)

interactions.label: vitamin_d
interactions.effect: With vitamin D supplements, blood calcium could rise too high.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor before vitamin D above usual amounts.

interactions.label: calcium
interactions.effect: Calcium supplements are listed as not mixing well with indapamide.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor before calcium supplements.

interactions.label: zinc
interactions.effect: These medicines increase zinc loss in urine.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor if a zinc check is needed.

interactions.label: magnesium
interactions.effect: These medicines increase magnesium loss in urine.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor about magnesium checks.

interactions.label: potassium
interactions.effect: These medicines increase potassium loss in urine and can cause low potassium.
interactions.action: Only take potassium if your doctor advises it.

interactions.label: licorice root
interactions.effect: Licorice can cause serious side effects, especially in people with high blood pressure.
interactions.action: Avoid licorice supplements.

medicines.name: Loop water tablets (for example furosemide, bumetanide)

interactions.label: potassium
interactions.effect: Supplements that raise potassium may not mix well with furosemide.
interactions.action: Only take potassium if your doctor advises it and checks your blood.

interactions.label: magnesium
interactions.effect: These medicines increase magnesium loss in urine.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor about magnesium checks.

interactions.label: vitamin_b1
interactions.effect: Furosemide can lower thiamin levels through urine.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor whether thiamin is needed.

interactions.label: licorice root
interactions.effect: Licorice can cause serious heart rhythm problems.
interactions.action: Avoid licorice supplements.

medicines.name: Bone medicines: bisphosphonates (for example alendronic acid, risedronate)

interactions.label: calcium
interactions.effect: The bone tablet works best on an empty stomach, so calcium and food at the same time get in the way.
interactions.action: Take the bone tablet first with plain tap water; wait at least 30 minutes before calcium, food or other medicines.

interactions.label: magnesium
interactions.effect: Magnesium supplements and antacids reduce absorption of these bone medicines.
interactions.action: Keep magnesium at least 2 hours away.

interactions.label: iron
interactions.effect: Supplements with iron are listed as something to tell your doctor about.
interactions.action: Tell your doctor; take iron at a different time of day.

interactions.label: zinc
interactions.effect: Supplements with zinc are listed as something to tell your doctor about.
interactions.action: Tell your doctor; take zinc at a different time of day.

interactions.label: all vitamins and supplements
interactions.effect: Vitamins, supplements and antacids taken at the same time can stop the medicine working.
interactions.action: Take them at least 30 minutes after the bone tablet.

medicines.name: SSRI and SNRI antidepressants (for example sertraline, citalopram, fluoxetine, venlafaxine)

interactions.label: St John's wort
interactions.effect: With some antidepressants it can cause serotonin-related side effects, which can be serious. National medicine advice says not to use it with sertraline, citalopram, fluoxetine or venlafaxine.
interactions.action: Do not take St John's wort with these medicines. Avoid it completely while on these medicines.

interactions.label: 5-HTP
interactions.effect: Raises serotonin. With these medicines there is a possible risk of serotonin syndrome, a serious reaction.
interactions.action: Do not take 5-HTP unless your doctor supervises it.

interactions.label: tryptophan
interactions.effect: Listed as possibly interacting with sertraline, fluoxetine and venlafaxine.
interactions.action: Do not take tryptophan unless your doctor agrees.

medicines.name: Hormonal contraceptive pills (for example the combined pill)

interactions.label: St John's wort
interactions.effect: Can weaken birth control pills, so pregnancy could happen.
interactions.action: Do not take it with the pill without advice; ask about other contraception.

interactions.label: vitamin_b12
interactions.effect: The combined pill can lower B12 blood test results without a real deficiency.
interactions.action: Tell your doctor you take the pill if your B12 is tested.

medicines.name: Steroid tablets (for example prednisolone, prednisone)

interactions.label: vitamin_d
interactions.effect: Steroids such as prednisone can lower vitamin D levels.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor if you need vitamin D, especially on long courses.

interactions.label: calcium
interactions.effect: Your doctor may advise a high-calcium diet or a calcium supplement.
interactions.action: Follow your doctor's advice on calcium.

interactions.label: potassium
interactions.effect: Your doctor may advise a high-potassium diet or a supplement.
interactions.action: Only take potassium if your doctor advises it.

interactions.label: St John's wort
interactions.effect: Listed as possibly interacting with prednisone.
interactions.action: Avoid unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: licorice root
interactions.effect: Interactions between licorice and corticosteroids have been reported.
interactions.action: Avoid licorice supplements.

medicines.name: Methotrexate

interactions.label: vitamin_b9
interactions.effect: Your doctor may prescribe folic acid with methotrexate. Do not take extra folic acid or folate from other products on top. If you take methotrexate for cancer, folate supplements could interfere with how it works.
interactions.action: Do not take folic acid or folate-containing vitamins unless your doctor says so. Ask your cancer doctor before any folate supplement.

interactions.label: alcohol
interactions.effect: Heavy drinking and liver disease matter with methotrexate.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor about the safe use of alcohol.

medicines.name: Anti-seizure medicines (for example carbamazepine, phenytoin, sodium valproate, lamotrigine)

interactions.label: vitamin_b9
interactions.effect: Some of these medicines lower folate, and folate supplements might lower the medicine level.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor before folic acid. If you are planning a pregnancy, a higher prescribed dose may be advised.

interactions.label: St John's wort
interactions.effect: Can weaken phenytoin and carbamazepine.
interactions.action: Do not take it with these medicines.

interactions.label: vitamin_b6
interactions.effect: High doses (200 mg a day) may lower phenytoin and phenobarbital levels.
interactions.action: Avoid high-dose B6 unless your doctor agrees.

interactions.label: vitamin_d
interactions.effect: Listed as possibly interacting with phenytoin.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor about vitamin D.

interactions.label: antacids
interactions.effect: Antacids with calcium, magnesium or aluminium are listed as possibly interacting with phenytoin.
interactions.action: Ask your pharmacist how to space them.

interactions.label: vitamin_b7
interactions.effect: Using these medicines for a year or more is linked to lower biotin levels.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor if this matters for you.

interactions.label: cannabidiol (CBD)
interactions.effect: Listed as possibly interacting with valproate.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor first.

interactions.label: ashwagandha
interactions.effect: Might interact with anti-seizure medicines.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor first.

medicines.name: Lithium

interactions.label: calcium
interactions.effect: Long-term lithium can raise blood calcium, and calcium supplements could add to this.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor before calcium supplements.

interactions.label: sodium bicarbonate
interactions.effect: Listed as possibly interacting with lithium.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor first.

interactions.label: herbal remedies and supplements
interactions.effect: There is not enough information to say they are safe with lithium.
interactions.action: Ask your doctor or pharmacist before any supplement.

interactions.label: caffeine
interactions.effect: Your doctor may want to know how much tea, coffee or cola you drink.
interactions.action: Talk to your doctor about caffeine drinks.

interactions.label: salt and fluids
interactions.effect: It is important to get the right amounts of fluid and salt while taking lithium.
interactions.action: Follow your doctor's advice on salt and fluids.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: all herbal and dietary supplements (default if no specific advice)
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Anaesthetists may ask you to stop supplements at least 2 weeks before. This is caution, not proof of harm. Always follow your own surgical team.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: garlic
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Garlic supplements may increase bleeding. A 2001 review advised stopping at least 7 days before; some teams ask for 2 weeks.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: ginkgo
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: A 2001 review advised stopping at least 36 hours before surgery because of possible bleeding. Some teams ask for 2 weeks.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: ginseng
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: May increase bleeding and lower blood sugar. A 2001 review advised stopping at least 7 days before.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: St John's wort
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Speeds up how the body clears many medicines used around surgery. A 2001 review advised stopping at least 5 days before.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: kava
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: May make anaesthetic drugs stronger. A 2001 review advised stopping at least 24 hours before; some teams ask for 2 weeks.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: valerian
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: May prolong anaesthesia. If possible taper it over the weeks before surgery; if not, a review advised continuing until surgery. Do not stop suddenly after long use.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: vitamin_e
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Often stopped before surgery because of a possible bleeding risk, but the evidence is weak: a small study found 800 IU a day for 2 weeks did not change bleeding time or platelet function.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: omega_3
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Evidence does not support stopping. In a large heart-surgery trial (OPERA), high-dose fish oil did not increase bleeding and fewer blood transfusions were needed. Follow your team's advice.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: turmeric
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Listed in guidance based on a 2021 expert consensus among supplements to hold 2 weeks before surgery, because of a theoretical bleeding risk.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: feverfew
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Listed in guidance based on a 2021 expert consensus among supplements to hold 2 weeks before surgery, because of a theoretical bleeding risk.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: saw palmetto
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Listed in guidance based on a 2021 expert consensus among supplements to hold 2 weeks before surgery, because of a theoretical bleeding risk.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: ginger (supplements)
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Some surgical centres list ginger among supplements to stop 2 weeks before surgery.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: echinacea
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: A 2001 review advised stopping as far ahead as possible, especially for people with liver problems or a transplant. 14 days is a practical default.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: ashwagandha
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Experts do not recommend ashwagandha for people about to have surgery. No exact stop time is given, so use the usual 2-week default unless told otherwise.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: melatonin
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Some surgical centres list it among supplements to stop 2 weeks before. Evidence of harm is lacking; ask your team.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: multivitamins
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Some surgical centres ask you to stop multivitamins 2 weeks before. Ask your own team.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: glucosamine and chondroitin
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Some surgical centres list them among supplements to stop 2 weeks before.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: iron
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Usually continued. If you have iron-deficiency anaemia, iron is advised before and after surgery.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: vitamin_d
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Some surgical centres list it as fine to continue before surgery.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: vitamin_c
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Some surgical centres list it as fine to continue before surgery.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: zinc
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Some surgical centres list it as fine to continue before surgery.

pauseBeforeSurgery.label: magnesium
pauseBeforeSurgery.why: Some surgical centres list it as fine to continue before surgery.
